name: Jeremiah
v: This is what the LORD says: Watch — I am rousing a destroying wind against Babylon, against those who live in Leb-kamai, the heart of my enemies.
I will send strangers to Babylon who will winnow her, who will strip her land bare. They will hem her in from every side on the day of her ruin.
Let no archer stretch his bow. Let no warrior strap on his armor. Spare none of her young men. Wipe out her entire army.
They will fall, slain, in the land of the Chaldeans, run through in her streets.
Israel and Judah are not abandoned by their God — not by the LORD of Armies — though their land overflowed with guilt against the Holy One of Israel.
Run from Babylon! Save your own skin! Don't go down with her in her ruin. This is the LORD's payback time — he is giving her what she earned.
Babylon was a gold cup in the LORD's hand, intoxicating the whole earth. The nations drank her wine and went mad.
Then suddenly — Babylon fell. Shattered. Wail over her. Get balm for her wounds. Maybe she can be healed.
We tried to heal Babylon, but she could not be healed. Leave her. Each of us, go home. Her judgment reaches to the heavens, towers up to the clouds.
The LORD has cleared us. Come — let's tell it in Zion, the work the LORD our God has done.
Sharpen the arrows! Fill the quivers! The LORD has stirred up the spirit of the kings of the Medes — his plan is Babylon, to wreck her. This is the LORD's vengeance, vengeance for his temple.
Raise the standard against Babylon's walls. Reinforce the watch. Post the sentries. Set the ambush. The LORD has both planned and done what he spoke against the people of Babylon.
You who live by mighty waters, rich in treasure — your end has come. The thread of your life is cut.
The LORD of Armies has sworn by himself: I will fill you with men like a swarm of locusts, and they will raise the victory cry over you.
He made the earth by his power, set the world in place by his wisdom, stretched out the heavens by his understanding.
When he thunders, the waters in the heavens roar. He lifts mist from the ends of the earth, sends lightning with the rain, brings the wind out from his storehouses.
Every human is a fool, without knowledge. Every goldsmith is shamed by his idol — those cast images are lies. There's no breath in them.
Worthless. A joke. When their judgment comes, they vanish.
Not so the Portion of Jacob — he is the Maker of everything, and Israel is the tribe of his inheritance. The LORD of Armies is his name.
You are my war-hammer, my weapon of war. With you I shatter nations. With you I destroy kingdoms.
With you I shatter horse and rider. With you I shatter chariot and driver.
With you I shatter man and woman. With you I shatter old and young. With you I shatter boy and girl.
With you I shatter shepherd and flock. With you I shatter farmer and team. With you I shatter governors and officials.
And right before your eyes I will repay Babylon and every Chaldean for all the evil they did in Zion. This is the LORD's word.
Look — I am against you, mountain of destruction, you who destroyed the whole earth. I will stretch out my hand against you, roll you down from the cliffs, turn you into a charred mountain.
No one will take a cornerstone from you, no foundation stone. You'll be desolation, forever. This is the LORD's word.

Raise a banner across the land! Sound the trumpet among the nations! Consecrate the nations against her. Summon the kingdoms — Ararat, Minni, Ashkenaz. Appoint a commander against her. Send up horses like bristling locusts.
Consecrate nations against her — the kings of the Medes, their governors and officials and every land they rule.
The earth shakes and writhes — the LORD's plans against Babylon stand: to make her land a wasteland with no one living there.
Babylon's warriors have stopped fighting. They sit in their strongholds. Their strength is dried up. They've become women. Her dwellings are torched, her gate-bars broken.
Runner races to meet runner, messenger to meet messenger, telling the king of Babylon: the city is taken from end to end.
The river crossings are seized. The marshes are burning. The soldiers panic.
This is what the LORD of Armies, the God of Israel, says: The daughter of Babylon is a threshing floor at harvest time — soon, very soon, her harvest will come.
Nebuchadnezzar of Babylon devoured me, crushed me, left me an empty vessel. He swallowed me like a sea-monster, gorged on my delicacies, then spat me out.
Let the violence done to me — to my own flesh — be on Babylon, says the woman of Zion. Let my blood be on the Chaldeans, says Jerusalem.
So this is what the LORD says: Watch — I am taking up your case. I will execute your vengeance. I will dry up her sea. I will parch her springs.
Babylon will become a heap of rubble, a haunt of jackals, an object of horror and hissing — empty, no one living there.
Her people roar together like lions. They growl like lion cubs.
When they're heated up, I'll set out their feast and get them drunk, until they're laughing — and then they'll fall into endless sleep and never wake. This is the LORD's word.
I'll lead them down to slaughter like lambs, like rams and goats.
How Sheshak is captured! The pride of all the earth, seized! What a horror Babylon has become among the nations!
The sea has surged over Babylon — its roaring waves have buried her.
Her cities are wasteland, a parched and arid land, a country no one lives in, where no human passes through.
I will punish Bel in Babylon. I will pull from his mouth what he swallowed. Nations will no longer stream to him. The wall of Babylon falls.
Come out of her, my people! Each of you — save your own life from the burning fury of the LORD.
Don't lose heart. Don't panic at the rumors running through the land — one rumor this year, another the next, violence in the land, ruler against ruler.
The days are coming when I will punish the idols of Babylon. Her whole land will be put to shame. Her slain will lie scattered through her streets.
Then heaven and earth and everything in them will shout for joy over Babylon — because the destroyers are coming from the north. This is the LORD's word.
Babylon must fall — because of the slain of Israel, just as the slain of all the earth fell because of Babylon.
You who escaped the sword — go. Don't stand still. Remember the LORD from far away. Let Jerusalem rise up in your hearts.
We are humiliated — we heard the insults. Shame covers our faces. Strangers walked into the holy places of the LORD's house.
So the days are coming, says the LORD, when I will punish her idols, and through her whole land the wounded will groan.
Even if Babylon climbs to the sky and fortifies her heights into the clouds, destroyers from me will reach her. This is the LORD's word.
Listen — screaming from Babylon. The crash of catastrophe from the land of the Chaldeans!
The LORD is laying Babylon waste, silencing her great noise. Their waves roar like crashing seas — the uproar of their voices rises.
A destroyer is coming against her — against Babylon. Her warriors will be captured, their bows snapped. The LORD is a God of payback. He pays in full.
I will make her officials and her wise men drunk — her governors, her officers, her warriors. They will sleep an endless sleep and never wake. So says the King, the LORD of Armies is his name.

This is what the LORD of Armies says: Babylon's massive walls will be leveled to the ground. Her towering gates will burn. The peoples labored for nothing. The nations exhausted themselves only to feed the fire.

These are the orders Jeremiah the prophet gave to Seraiah son of Neriah, son of Mahseiah, when Seraiah went with King Zedekiah of Judah to Babylon in the fourth year of his reign. Seraiah was the quartermaster.
Jeremiah had written in a single scroll every disaster that would come on Babylon — all these words written against Babylon.
Jeremiah told Seraiah: When you reach Babylon, read aloud every word in this scroll.
Then say: LORD, you yourself have spoken against this place — to cut it off, so no one will live in it, neither human nor animal. It will be desolation forever.
When you finish reading the scroll, tie a stone to it and throw it into the Euphrates.

Then say: This is how Babylon will sink — and never rise — because of the disaster I am bringing on her. They will be exhausted.

The words of Jeremiah end here.

com.d:
# Jeremiah 51: The Unstoppable Justice of God

When kingdoms rise and nations boast of their power and permanence, God reminds us through Jeremiah that no earthly empire is ultimately beyond His reach or accountability. This sweeping chapter proclaims that Babylon, seemingly invincible in its pride, will fall because the God of Israel is working out His purposes with relentless faithfulness.

Jeremiah's prophecy against Babylon doesn't emerge from mere political prediction but from his conviction that God is actively judging nations that rebel against Him and oppress His people. The prophet uses vivid imagery—a destroying wind, the archer missing no mark, the earth quaking—to show that divine justice is as real and unstoppable as natural forces. What strikes the heart is that even when God's people feel abandoned and defeated in exile, they are not forgotten. God hasn't abandoned His purposes; He's working behind the scenes in ways that may take years to unfold.

This passage speaks powerfully to those who suffer under oppression or injustice. When we watch evil flourish and wickedness prosper, it's easy to despair and wonder if God still governs the world. Jeremiah reminds us that apparent permanence is deceptive. Empires crumble. Oppressors fall. God's patience isn't weakness; it's the slow, inevitable work of justice that no human power can ultimately resist. The exiles clinging to their faith were invited to trust that their suffering had meaning within God's larger story.

For contemporary disciples, this passage calls us to think differently about power and permanence. We live in a world that constantly tempts us to fear human authorities or to build our security on earthly foundations. Yet Jeremiah's witness invites us to align ourselves with God's kingdom, which outlasts every human regime and cannot be shaken.

What earthly power or circumstance tempts you to forget that God's kingdom is ultimately secure and unstoppable? How might your anxieties shift if you truly rested in His eternal sovereignty?
com.s:
Jeremiah 51 constitutes the second half of the extended oracle against Babylon that begins in chapter 50, representing one of the most substantial prophetic pronouncements against a foreign nation in the Hebrew Bible. Composed during the tumultuous final years of Judah's existence as an independent kingdom, this chapter reflects the complex theological task facing Jeremiah: explaining how Babylon could simultaneously serve as Yahweh's instrument of judgment against Judah while itself remaining subject to divine retribution for its hubris and cruelty.

The chapter employs the term *mashḥît* (destroyer) repeatedly, presenting Babylon's destruction as divinely orchestrated vengeance. The Hebrew *nāqām* (vengeance) appears with particular theological weight, signifying not petty retaliation but the restoration of cosmic justice. Yahweh's vengeance represents the vindication of his temple and people, themes that resonate throughout the chapter's martial imagery. The designation of the Medes as agents of destruction situates the prophecy within the geopolitical realities of the sixth century, though the actual fall of Babylon to Cyrus in 539 BCE occurred with minimal military engagement, creating an interpretive tension that scholars continue to debate.

Structurally, the chapter alternates between divine speech and prophetic proclamation, building toward the dramatic symbolic action in verses 59-64, where Seraiah is commanded to read Jeremiah's words in Babylon and then sink the scroll in the Euphrates, enacting Babylon's irreversible submersion. The term *mĕṣûlâ* (depths) employed here echoes exodus traditions, suggesting a typological reversal wherein the oppressor nation now experiences the fate once reserved for Egypt.

The chapter's canonical placement immediately before the historical appendix of chapter 52 creates deliberate theological framing, positioning Babylon's prophesied fall as the interpretive lens through which readers understand Jerusalem's destruction. Within the broader prophetic corpus, Jeremiah 51 shares thematic and linguistic connections with Isaiah's Babylon oracles, though scholars disagree whether this represents literary dependence or common prophetic tradition. The chapter's extensive quotation and reformulation of earlier biblical materials—particularly from Jeremiah's own oracles and the Psalms—demonstrates sophisticated scribal activity, suggesting editorial expansion over time while preserving the essential prophetic message of Babylon's ultimate accountability before Israel's God.
com.p:
Jeremiah 51 thunders forth from approximately 593 BC, penned during the final desperate years of Judah's existence as Babylon's vassal, yet its prophetic gaze extends far beyond the immediate horizon. The chapter was written roughly a half-century before Babylon's actual fall to the Medes and Persians in 539 BC, making it a stunning example of predictive prophecy fulfilled in history—yet containing eschatological dimensions that reach into the end of the age. Within the grand redemptive arc, this oracle stands at the threshold of Exile, that dark corridor between Kingdom and Restoration, when God's people would learn in Babylonian captivity that their God reigns sovereign over all empires.

The prophetic burden against Babylon unfolds as divine vengeance for covenant violence. Babylon had been God's instrument of judgment—His "war club" as chapter 51 declares—yet the empire exceeded its mandate, showing no mercy and desecrating Yahweh's temple. Here emerges a pattern repeated throughout Scripture: God uses pagan powers to discipline His people, then judges those same powers for their cruelty and pride. Assyria learned this lesson; Babylon would learn it; Rome would learn it; and the final Babylon of Revelation will learn it when Christ returns.

The typological significance proves profound. Babylon transcends geography to become the archetype of all human systems arrayed against God's kingdom. When Jeremiah commands God's people to "flee from Babylon" and "save your lives," the language reverberates into the New Testament, where John echoes this very summons in Revelation 18: "Come out of her, my people." Ancient Babylon foreshadows the great prostitute drunk on the blood of saints, that final world system intoxicated by its own magnificence, declaring "I sit as queen." The fall of historical Babylon in 539 BC serves as down payment and guarantee of the ultimate Babylon's destruction.

The oracle's climactic imagery—Babylon sinking like a stone into the Euphrates, never to rise—finds its mirror in Revelation 18, where a mighty angel hurls a great millstone into the sea, declaring Babylon's eternal ruin. What Jeremiah saw in shadow, John saw in full apocalyptic color.

For the church dwelling between the advents, this chapter speaks with urgent relevance. Believers are called to identify Babylon's spirit wherever human pride, materialism, and persecution of the saints converge—and to maintain their exodus identity, living as strangers whose citizenship belongs to the city God is building, the New Jerusalem descending from heaven.
